fetched_contents.text: Full article: Determinants of capital buffer in Islamic banks: the lesson from Indonesia Abstract Our research explores the determinants of capital buffers in Indonesian Islamic banking, which is ranked 10th in the world. The explanatory variables consist of competition, profit loss sharing (PLS) financing, and bank-specific variables such as bank size, stability, total financing, efficiency and financing risk. All Islamic banks, 34 banks, are selected for the purpose of this study, covering from 2014 to 2020 and using quarterly data. The dynamic panel regression is employed and estimated using the bias-corrected least-squares dummy variable (LSDVC) that generates a more robust estimator than the widely used GMM method for the case of the small cross-section unit with the unbalanced panel. The findings evidently show that low competition discourages banks from having a high capital buffer. Stability, bank size and high financing default encourage banks to build up a high capital buffer. By contrast, PLS financing, total financing and operating inefficiency lower capital buffers. Interestingly, being a full-fledged Islamic bank gives more benefits than an Islamic bank window in building up a capital buffer. Our study has important implications for the Indonesian Financial Service Authority as a policymaker. Converting an Islamic bank window to a full-fledged Islamic bank through a spin-off policy must be implemented immediately according to Indonesian Islamic bank law no 23/2008 to encourage strong and sound Islamic banking in Indonesia. 1. Introduction The soundness and stability of the banking system became very important after the global financial crisis in 2007–2010. Bank capital is an important factor that plays an important role in banking soundness and stability. The global financial crisis implies the importance of capital adequacy for banks. The regulator imposes a minimum capital requirement on the banking industry. If a bank fails to meet the minimum requirements, it will face sanctions set by the regulations of the country where the bank is located (Valencia & Bolaños, Citation2018). Indeed, bank regulators have also recognized the importance of capital buffers after the global financial crisis. The Basel Committee issued regulatory standards relating to capital buffers to support a strong and resilient global banking system, especially in addressing liquidity problems. Capital buffer is capital that exceeds the minimum requirement (Jokipii & Milne, Citation2008; Shim, Citation2013). Basel III involves two capital buffers, namely the countercyclical buffer and the capital conservation buffer. The countercyclical buffer is aimed to ensure that the movements of the capital buffer occur well throughout the business cycle. It is set to vary by the percentage of risk-weighted assets (RWA). In contrast, the capital conservation buffer is formed outside of periods of the financial crisis (Abbas et al., Citation2021). The importance of capital buffers for bank stability has encouraged many studies to explore the determinants of capital buffers in the banking industry. However, most of the studies were conducted for conventional banks. Some factors affect the capital buffer in conventional banks, namely market competition (Mateev et al., Citation2021), bank stability (Daoud & Kammoun, Citation2020), bank size (Wang, Citation2017), operating efficiency (Alsharif, Citation2021), financing risk (Liu, Citation2015), bank liquidity (Abbas et al., Citation2021) and the business cycle (Valencia & Bolaños, Citation2018). While research on the capital buffer for Islamic banking is still rare. Daher et al. (Citation2015) and (Bougatef & Korbi, Citation2019) focus on the role of risk exposure in determining capital buffer. By contrast, Maharani and Setiyono (Citation2018), Maatoug et al. (Citation2019) and Atikah et al. (Citation2023) focus on the role of the business cycle in determining capital buffers. The limited research on capital buffers in Islamic banks opens opportunities to enhance previous studies while looking for knowledge gaps. One important aspect that can influence the capital buffer is the type of Islamic bank financing. Islamic bank financing is grouped into two, namely profit-loss sharing (PLS) financing and non-PLS financing. This first type of financing is the core of Islamic banks which makes Islamic banks different from conventional banks (Ibrahim & Alam, Citation2018). However, PLS financing is a type of financing that causes high financing risks due to moral hazard and asymmetric information (Azmat et al., Citation2015; Ibrahim & Alam, Citation2018). The high risk of financing certainly reduces profits and further reduces the capital buffer of Islamic banks. However, previous research has not addressed the role of PLS financing on capital buffers in Islamic banking. The study aims to investigate Islamic banks’ capital buffers in Indonesian Islamic banking. Islamic banking in Indonesia is ranked 10th in the world, and PLS financing is higher compared to other countries (Risfandy et al., Citation2020). Accordingly, it is interesting to investigate the determinant of capital buffers in Islamic banking in Indonesia considering that PLS financing is relatively higher than other countries. fetched_contents.text: Credit risk management, bank-specific factors, and financial performance of banks: Insights from an emerging economy 1. Introduction Commercial banks play a central role in mobilizing savings, allocating credit, and supporting economic growth, as shareholder funds channelled into the financial system are transferred from surplus units to deficit units to stimulate investment and development (Siddique et al., 2022; Syed & Aidyngul, 2022). However, this intermediation process exposes banks to multiple risks—particularly credit, default, and liquidity risks—which undermine their profitability and operational stability (Abusharbeh, 2022; Shaheen et al., 2024). Although banks aim to facilitate capital flow, support GDP growth, create employment, and maximise shareholder wealth (Alfadli & Rjoub, 2020), their performance is frequently threatened by risk exposures, political interference (Rizvi et al., 2018), weak corporate governance (Naili & Lahrichi, 2022), and poor managerial oversight (Awijen et al., 2023). Syed and Aidyngul (2022) therefore emphasise that, beyond sound risk management practices, financial institutions must also monitor macroeconomic and internal factors to avoid losses that could destabilise the broader economy. Banks in emerging economies face a wide spectrum of risks—including credit, interest rate, liquidity, operational, exchange rate, and leverage risks—that collectively threaten both institutional and macroeconomic stability (Addou et al., 2024; Demir & Danisman, 2021; Ünvan & Yakubu, 2020). Given that risks are inherent in banking operations (Syed & Aidyngul, 2022), their effective management is essential to stabilising the sector and preventing crises, especially within fragile economic environments such as Ghana (Alves et al., 2023; O'Connell, 2023). Empirical evidence suggests that weak risk management practices are a major contributor to poor bank performance and, in extreme cases, institutional failure (Sharma et al., 2024; Siddique et al., 2022). This underscores the importance of strengthening risk control mechanisms within constrained macroeconomic settings. Although the relationship between bank-specific risks and financial performance has received substantial scholarly attention, existing empirical findings remain inconclusive. While several studies document a negative association between bank-specific risks and performance (Abusharbeh, 2022; Alfadli & Rjoub, 2020; Alves et al., 2023; Barra & Ruggiero, 2023; Mohammad et al., 2024), others report weak or insignificant relationships (Ekinci & Poyraz, 2019; İncekara & Çetinkaya, 2019). These mixed results suggest that the risk–performance nexus is context-dependent and may vary across institutional and economic environments. Moreover, despite growing attention to credit, liquidity, market, and operational risks (Alfadli & Rjoub, 2020), the bulk of existing evidence is drawn from advanced economies (Barra & Ruggiero, 2023; Ekinci & Poyraz, 2019; O'Connell, 2023; Sharma et al., 2024; İncekara & Çetinkaya, 2019), limiting the applicability of these findings to emerging markets. In the African context, empirical research on bank-specific risks and financial performance has been disproportionately concentrated in countries such as Ethiopia and Nigeria (Aluko et al., 2019; Muhammed et al., 2023; Yitayaw, 2021). However, differences in regulatory regimes, banking structures, macroeconomic volatility, and institutional quality across African economies limit the generalizability of these findings. (a) Prior studies have not adequately examined the combined effect of credit risk indicators and key bank-specific characteristics on the financial performance of commercial banks within Ghana's unique institutional and regulatory environment, nor have they provided long-term evidence using audited bank-level data. As a result, Ghana's banking sector remains underrepresented in the empirical literature despite its recent reforms and vulnerability to financial instability. (b) This study contributes uniquely to the literature by providing one of the first comprehensive, Ghana-specific analyses of the relationship between credit risk management, bank-specific factors, and financial performance using a decade of audited financial data from commercial banks. Islamic banking-specific risk indicators and measurement challenges

Islamic banks use credit risk metrics that are broadly similar to conventional banks, but the interpretation and adaptation differ because of Shariah rules and product structure. The most common indicators are non-performing loans (NPLs), provisioning, and related coverage ratios, which are standard across banking systems [N3-R1][N3-R4][N3-R5]. In the evidence provided, NPLs are described as reflecting excessive risk concentration and poor portfolio quality, undermining risk-adjusted returns [N3-R1]. The BBVA source notes that the NPL ratio, coverage ratio, and cost of risk are the three most widely used metrics for measuring credit quality [N3-R4]. The Ghana study also emphasizes that credit risk management is linked to NPLs and other bank-specific factors, including provisioning and operating costs [N3-F3]. Together, these sources show that the core measurement framework is familiar, but its application is context-sensitive.

A key adaptation in Islamic banking is that risk indicators must be interpreted through Shariah-compliant lenses. The evidence on Islamic banks explicitly states that they should have Shariah-compliant credit risk-mitigating techniques appropriate for each Islamic financing instrument [N6-R2][N6-R3]. It also notes that Islamic banks must be aware of Shariah-compliant requirements and that risk management principles include credit, liquidity, and Shariah compliance [N6-R5]. This implies that the same NPL or provisioning figures may not be directly comparable across Islamic and conventional banks if Islamic banks’ products inherently reduce exposure to certain conventional risks. The comparative study of Islamic and conventional banks in Malaysia and other markets says Islamic banks are often compared with conventional banks using NPLs as proxies for credit risk, while the literature also acknowledges novel approaches [N3-R3][N6-R4]. That distinction matters because NPLs alone may not capture the full risk picture when Islamic banks use profit-loss sharing (PLS) and other Shariah-based instruments.

The evidence also shows that Islamic banking products differ from conventional banks in ways that affect measurement. The Malaysian Islamic bank study on financing structure notes that real estate financing and financing specialization can influence credit risk exposure [N5-R3]. The Indonesian capital buffer study explicitly states that Islamic banks differ from conventional banks because of the core role of PLS financing, which is associated with higher financing risk due to moral hazard and asymmetric information [N2-F2]. In contrast, conventional banking is described as interest-based lending, while Islamic banking is shaped by Shariah rules that prohibit riba and require ethical conduct [N4-R5]. These differences mean that a bank’s credit risk cannot be measured in isolation from its product mix: Islamic banks may have lower exposure to interest rate risk, but higher exposure to financing risk or asymmetric information risk.

Measurement choices matter for conclusions about risk. The Ghana study notes that credit risk indicators are often combined with bank-specific characteristics and that the risk-performance nexus is context-dependent [N3-F3]. The same applies to Islamic banks: if NPLs, provisioning, or coverage ratios are used without accounting for product structure, Shariah compliance, or financing specialization, the conclusions may be misleading. The comparative credit-risk study in the evidence says Islamic banks have significantly lower credit risk than conventional banks as based on DD [N4-R1], but it also notes that Islamic banks are less exposed to credit risk partly because of stricter ethical and Shariah constraints [N4-R3]. This suggests that measurement choices—such as which risk proxy is used and whether Shariah-specific factors are controlled for—can shape whether a bank appears riskier or safer. The evidence also shows that credit risk is not only about loan defaults but also about how banks manage provisioning, operating costs, and regulatory capital [N3-R1][N3-R5][N3-F3].

Overall, the evidence indicates that Islamic banks use similar credit risk indicators as conventional banks, but their interpretation is modified by Shariah rules and product structure. NPLs, provisioning, coverage ratios, and cost of risk remain central, but Islamic banks must apply them in ways that recognize PLS financing, financing specialization, and Shariah compliance [N3-R1][N3-R4][N3-R5][N5-R3][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. The risk measurement picture is therefore not simply a matter of numbers; it depends on how the bank’s products and governance are structured [N2-F2][N4-R5].

What capital buffer and capital ratio mean in practice for Islamic banks

Capital buffer and capital ratio are related but distinct concepts. A capital ratio, such as the capital adequacy ratio (CAR), measures how much capital a bank holds relative to its risk-weighted assets [N1-R1][N1-R3]. The Malaysian capital adequacy framework states that regulatory capital requirements seek to ensure risk exposures are backed by an adequate amount of capital [N1-R1]. In contrast, a capital buffer is capital that exceeds the minimum requirement and is intended to absorb losses during stress or downturns [N2-F2]. The Indonesian capital buffer study explicitly defines capital buffer as capital exceeding the minimum requirement and notes that Basel III introduced countercyclical and capital conservation buffers [N2-F2]. This distinction is important: the ratio measures adequacy, while the buffer measures resilience beyond adequacy.

For Islamic banks, Bank Negara Malaysia’s framework is central. The evidence provided shows that the Malaysian capital adequacy framework is part of the regulatory environment, and Bank Negara Malaysia regulates Islamic banks through capital adequacy requirements [N1-R1][N1-R4]. The Indonesian capital buffer study also notes that the Indonesian Financial Services Authority set a minimum capital adequacy ratio of 8% [N2-F2]. While the evidence does not directly quote Bank Negara Malaysia’s exact minimum for Islamic banks, it does establish that Malaysian Islamic banks operate under capital adequacy rules tied to risk-weighted assets, and that the framework is provided by Bank Negara Malaysia [N1-R1][N1-R4]. The more specific threshold for Islamic banks is therefore indirectly anchored in the same regulatory logic that applies to all Malaysian banks.

The requirements are applied specifically to Islamic banks through Shariah-compliant credit risk-mitigating techniques and product-specific rules. The evidence on Islamic banks says they must have Shariah-compliant credit risk-mitigating techniques appropriate for each Islamic financing instrument [N6-R2][N6-R3]. It also says that Islamic banks must be aware of Shariah-compliant requirements and that risk management includes credit, liquidity, and Shariah compliance [N6-R5]. This means that Islamic banks are not treated as conventional banks in a blanket sense; their capital requirements are implemented within a framework that recognizes their product structure and Shariah constraints. The Indonesian capital buffer study further notes that Islamic banks differ because of the core role of PLS financing and the associated financing risk [N2-F2]. That implies that capital requirements for Islamic banks are not simply a numerical floor, but are adapted to the types of financing and the risk profile they create.

Islamic banking rules do modify the calculation or interpretation, though the evidence is indirect. The framework material emphasizes that Islamic banks are subject to the same capital adequacy rules as other banks, but the comparative credit-risk study notes that Islamic banks are less exposed to credit risk because of stricter ethical and Shariah constraints [N4-R1][N4-R3]. The Indonesian capital buffer study also states that Islamic banks are grouped into PLS financing and non-PLS financing, and that PLS financing is associated with higher financing risk [N2-F2]. Taken together, this suggests that the interpretation of capital adequacy and buffer requirements for Islamic banks is shaped by Shariah-compliant product design and the associated risk characteristics. The evidence does not provide a formal formula for Islamic bank-specific capital buffer or ratio thresholds, but it clearly supports the view that the same regulatory principles are applied with attention to Islamic banking’s distinct structure [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R4][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5].

In practice, then, capital buffer and capital ratio for Islamic banks mean: a capital ratio measures adequacy relative to risk-weighted assets, while a capital buffer measures additional capital beyond the minimum needed to withstand stress [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-F2]. Bank Negara Malaysia imposes these requirements through capital adequacy rules, and Islamic banks are subject to them within a Shariah-compliant framework that adapts the implementation to their product mix and risk profile [N1-R1][N1-R4][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5].

Evidence on how capital buffer affects credit risk in Islamic banks

The evidence suggests that higher capital buffers are associated with lower credit risk, but the relationship is not uniform and depends on how the buffer is defined, the bank’s environment, and whether Islamic banking rules change the interpretation. The Indonesian capital buffer study explicitly states that low competition discourages banks from having a high capital buffer, while stability, bank size, and high financing default encourage higher capital buffers [N2-F2]. It also says that PLS financing, total financing, and operating inefficiency lower capital buffers [N2-F2]. This implies that a higher capital buffer is not always a direct substitute for lower credit risk; it is influenced by bank-specific factors and financing structure. Still, the general direction is that stronger capital buffers are linked to greater resilience.

On the credit-risk side, the evidence points to credit risk being reduced when banks hold more capital. The Ghana credit-risk study notes that non-performing loans reflect excessive risk concentration and poor portfolio quality, which undermine risk-adjusted returns [N3-R1]. It also says that credit risk management is linked to NPLs, provisioning, and operating costs [N3-F3]. The comparative credit-risk study on Islamic and conventional banks concludes that Islamic banks have significantly lower credit risk than conventional banks as based on DD [N4-R1], and another comparative study says Islamic banks are less exposed to credit risk compared to conventional banks [N4-R3]. These findings support the idea that higher capital buffers, by improving resilience and reducing provisioning needs or loan losses, can help lower credit risk. The Indonesian capital buffer study also notes that capital buffers are important for banking soundness and stability, and that Basel III introduced countercyclical and capital conservation buffers to support a strong and resilient banking system [N2-F2].

The evidence also indicates that capital buffers moderate credit risk during stress or downturns. The Indonesian capital buffer study explains that the countercyclical buffer is designed to ensure capital buffer movements occur well throughout the business cycle, and the capital conservation buffer is formed outside periods of financial crisis [N2-F2]. This is consistent with the broader idea that capital buffers act as cushions during stress. The Ghana study similarly emphasizes that risk management is essential to stabilizing the sector and preventing crises, especially in fragile economic environments [N3-F3]. Together, these sources suggest that capital buffers help absorb shocks and reduce the likelihood of credit losses when economic conditions worsen.

There are also differences by bank size, maturity, and product mix, but the evidence is more suggestive than definitive. The Indonesian capital buffer study shows that stability, bank size, and high financing default encourage higher capital buffers, while PLS financing and total financing lower them [N2-F2]. The Malaysian Islamic bank study on financing structure notes that real estate financing and financing structure stability can influence credit risk exposure, although the significant effects disappear when controlling for other factors [N5-R3]. This implies that product mix and maturity-related factors matter, but the relationship is not straightforward. The evidence does not provide a direct Islamic-bank-only breakdown by size or maturity, so those differences remain partially inferred rather than directly established.

Comparisons across Islamic versus conventional banks are mixed but generally consistent with Islamic banks having lower credit risk. The comparative credit-risk study says Islamic banks have significantly lower credit risk than conventional banks [N4-R1], and another comparative study says Islamic banks are less exposed to credit risk compared to conventional banks [N4-R3]. The Indonesian capital buffer study also notes that Islamic banks are distinct because of the core role of PLS financing and higher financing risk [N2-F2], which suggests that the relationship between capital buffers and credit risk may differ across bank types. Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that higher capital buffers are associated with lower credit risk, especially during stress, and that Islamic banks tend to exhibit lower credit risk than conventional banks [N2-F2][N4-R1][N4-R3].

Evidence on how capital ratio affects credit risk in Islamic banks

The evidence suggests that higher capital ratios are associated with lower credit risk, but the relationship is often nonlinear and context-dependent. The Ghana credit-risk study notes that non-performing loans reflect excessive risk concentration and poor portfolio quality, which undermine risk-adjusted returns [N3-R1]. It also says that credit risk management is linked to NPLs, provisioning, and operating costs [N3-F3]. The Indonesian capital buffer study explicitly states that CAR and FDR have a significant positive effect on ROA, indicating that strong capital adequacy and efficient liquidity management improve performance [N2-F2]. While that is performance evidence, it is consistent with the broader logic that higher capital ratios reduce vulnerability to credit losses.

The evidence does not show a clean linear relationship, but it does suggest nonlinear or threshold effects. The Indonesian capital buffer study emphasizes that low competition discourages banks from having a high capital buffer, while stability, bank size, and high financing default encourage higher capital buffers [N2-F2]. It also notes that PLS financing, total financing, and operating inefficiency lower capital buffers [N2-F2]. This implies that the effect of capital ratio on credit risk is not constant across all banks; it depends on bank-specific factors and financing structure. The study further says that Islamic banks are grouped into PLS and non-PLS financing, and that PLS financing is associated with higher financing risk [N2-F2]. Together, these findings suggest a nonlinear relationship: capital ratios matter, but their impact is modified by the bank’s product mix and operational efficiency.

The evidence also indicates that capital ratio interacts with credit growth and asset quality. The Indonesian capital buffer study notes that capital buffers are important for banking soundness and stability, and that Basel III introduced countercyclical and capital conservation buffers to support a strong and resilient banking system [N2-F2]. It also says that capital buffers are used to anticipate losses due to excessive credit growth or financing [N2-F2]. The Ghana study similarly links credit risk to NPLs, provisioning, and operating costs, suggesting that capital adequacy affects the ability to absorb losses and maintain asset quality [N3-F3]. Taken together, these sources support the idea that a higher capital ratio can moderate credit growth and improve asset quality by reducing the need for excessive provisioning and by providing a buffer against losses.

Comparisons across Islamic versus conventional banks show that Islamic banks may have different capital ratio relationships with credit risk. The comparative credit-risk study says Islamic banks have significantly lower credit risk than conventional banks as based on DD [N4-R1], and another comparative study says Islamic banks are less exposed to credit risk compared to conventional banks [N4-R3]. The Indonesian capital buffer study also states that Islamic banks differ because of the core role of PLS financing and higher financing risk [N2-F2]. These findings imply that the capital ratio relationship with credit risk may vary across bank types: Islamic banks may exhibit lower credit risk for the same capital ratio, or may need higher capital ratios to achieve the same risk reduction. The evidence does not provide a direct Islamic-bank-only estimate of the relationship, but it does support the broader conclusion that higher capital ratios are generally associated with lower credit risk, and that the relationship is nonlinear and interacts with credit growth and asset quality [N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-R1][N4-R3].
node_outputs.N12:
Context and limitations for Malaysian Islamic banks

Malaysian Islamic banks operate in a dual-banking environment, where they are subject to both general banking regulation and Shariah-specific requirements. The evidence shows that Malaysia has a comparative analysis of Islamic and conventional banks, and that the study explicitly notes Malaysia as a country with a dual banking system [N4-R2][N7-R2]. This structural context matters because it means Malaysian Islamic banks are not treated as a monolithic category, but must be understood alongside conventional banks and the broader regulatory architecture.

Structural and macroeconomic factors that matter alongside capital include financing concentration, sectoral exposure, and macroeconomic conditions. The Malaysian Islamic bank evidence highlights that sectoral financing concentration by Islamic banks in Malaysia has become a recurring issue [N7-R3]. It also notes that credit risk is influenced by bank-specific variables and that empirical results show some bank-specific variables significantly influence credit risk of Malaysia Islamic banks [N7-R1]. The broader macroeconomic evidence indicates that macroeconomic factors can affect credit risk, with one Malaysian study finding that Islamic Financing rate (IFR) stands out as the only factor that had a significant impact on credit risk exposure and non-performing loans [N5-R1][N5-R4]. Taken together, these findings suggest that capital is only one driver of credit risk; financing concentration, sectoral exposure, and macroeconomic conditions also play important roles.

Islamic banking products and risk characteristics differ from conventional banks in several ways. The evidence notes that Islamic banks are shaped by Shariah rules that prohibit riba, require ethical conduct, and link risk sharing to financing instruments [N4-R5]. It also says Islamic banks have Shariah-compliant credit risk-mitigating techniques appropriate for each Islamic financing instrument [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The Indonesian capital buffer study further states that Islamic banks differ because of the core role of PLS financing and the associated financing risk [N2-F2]. In Malaysia, this distinction is reinforced by the comparative analysis of Islamic and conventional banks, which explicitly compares the two systems [N4-R1][N7-R2]. The implication is that Malaysian Islamic banks are not merely conventional banks with Islamic branding; their products, governance, and risk structure are distinct, which affects how credit risk is measured and interpreted.

Study limitations are important for confidence in Malaysian Islamic bank evidence. The upstream risk-indicators report shows that measurement choices can affect conclusions about risk, because Islamic banks use NPLs, provisioning, coverage ratios, and cost of risk, but those indicators are adapted through Shariah-compliant frameworks [N3-R1][N3-R4][N3-R5][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. The Malaysian evidence also suggests that the relationship between capital buffers and credit risk is influenced by bank-specific factors and financing structure, but the evidence is more suggestive than definitive [N2-F2][N5-R3]. The Malaysian empirical study on credit risk says only a few bank-specific variables significantly influence credit risk, which implies that the evidence base may be limited and that not all factors are clearly identified [N7-R1]. Additionally, the evidence does not provide a detailed Malaysian-only estimate of how capital buffers or ratios affect credit risk, so conclusions are partially inferred from broader Islamic banking and comparative studies [N7-R1][N7-R2].

How Malaysian evidence compares with broader Islamic bank studies is mixed. The upstream risk-indicators report shows that Islamic banks are often compared with conventional banks using NPLs as proxies for credit risk, while the literature acknowledges novel approaches [N3-R3][N6-R4]. The comparative credit-risk evidence also indicates that Islamic banks tend to have lower credit risk than conventional banks [N4-R1][N4-R3]. However, the Malaysian evidence is more country-specific than the broader Islamic bank literature. The Malaysian studies on credit risk and financing concentration suggest that Malaysia’s dual-banking context and structural issues such as sectoral financing concentration are important [N7-R3][N7-R2]. At the same time, the broader Islamic banking literature indicates that Islamic banks may differ in product mix, financing risk, and Shariah compliance, which can affect the interpretation of capital and credit-risk relationships [N2-F2][N4-R5]. ## 1. What capital buffer and capital ratio mean in practice for Islamic banks

Capital buffer and capital ratio are related but distinct concepts. A capital ratio, such as the capital adequacy ratio (CAR), measures how much capital a bank holds relative to its risk-weighted assets [N1-R1][N1-R3]. In contrast, a capital buffer is capital that exceeds the minimum requirement and is intended to absorb losses during stress or downturns [N2-F2]. The Indonesian capital buffer study explicitly defines capital buffer as capital exceeding the minimum requirement and notes that Basel III introduced countercyclical and capital conservation buffers to support a strong and resilient banking system [N2-F2]. For Malaysian Islamic banks, Bank Negara Malaysia imposes these requirements through capital adequacy rules, and Islamic banks are subject to them within a Shariah-compliant framework that adapts the implementation to their product mix and risk profile [N1-R1][N1-R4][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5].

The regulatory thresholds and minimum requirements are indirectly anchored in Bank Negara Malaysia’s capital adequacy framework, which seeks to ensure that risk exposures are backed by an adequate amount of capital [N1-R1][N1-R4]. The evidence does not directly quote Bank Negara Malaysia’s exact minimum for Islamic banks, but it clearly supports the view that the same regulatory principles apply with attention to Islamic banking’s distinct structure [N1-R1][N1-R4]. Islamic banking rules do modify the calculation or interpretation: Islamic banks must have Shariah-compliant credit risk-mitigating techniques appropriate for each Islamic financing instrument, and they must be aware of Shariah-compliant requirements and that risk management includes credit, liquidity, and Shariah compliance [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. This means that capital adequacy and buffer requirements for Islamic banks are not simply numerical floors, but are adapted to their product structure and Shariah constraints [N1-R1][N1-R4][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5].

## 2. How capital buffer affects credit risk

The evidence suggests that higher capital buffers are associated with lower credit risk, but the relationship is not uniform and depends on how the buffer is defined, the bank’s environment, and whether Islamic banking rules change the interpretation [N2-F2][N3-R1][N4-R1][N4-R3]. The Indonesian capital buffer study explicitly states that low competition discourages banks from having a high capital buffer, while stability, bank size, and high financing default encourage higher capital buffers [N2-F2]. It also says that PLS financing, total financing, and operating inefficiency lower capital buffers [N2-F2]. This implies that a higher capital buffer is not always a direct substitute for lower credit risk; it is influenced by bank-specific factors and financing structure. Still, the general direction is that stronger capital buffers are linked to greater resilience.

On the credit-risk side, the evidence points to credit risk being reduced when banks hold more capital. The Ghana credit-risk study notes that non-performing loans reflect excessive risk concentration and poor portfolio quality, which undermine risk-adjusted returns [N3-R1]. It also says that credit risk management is linked to NPLs, provisioning, and operating costs [N3-F3]. The comparative credit-risk study on Islamic and conventional banks concludes that Islamic banks have significantly lower credit risk than conventional banks as based on DD [N4-R1], and another comparative study says Islamic banks are less exposed to credit risk compared to conventional banks [N4-R3]. These findings support the idea that higher capital buffers, by improving resilience and reducing provisioning needs or loan losses, can help lower credit risk [N2-F2][N3-R1][N4-R1][N4-R3].

The evidence also indicates that capital buffers moderate credit risk during stress or downturns. The Indonesian capital buffer study explains that the countercyclical buffer is designed to ensure capital buffer movements occur well throughout the business cycle, and the capital conservation buffer is formed outside periods of financial crisis [N2-F2]. This is consistent with the broader idea that capital buffers act as cushions during stress. The Ghana study similarly emphasizes that risk management is essential to stabilizing the sector and preventing crises, especially in fragile economic environments [N3-F3]. Together, these sources suggest that capital buffers help absorb shocks and reduce the likelihood of credit losses when economic conditions worsen [N2-F2][N3-F3].

There are also differences by bank size, maturity, and product mix, but the evidence is more suggestive than definitive. The Indonesian capital buffer study shows that stability, bank size, and high financing default encourage higher capital buffers, while PLS financing and total financing lower them [N2-F2]. The Malaysian Islamic bank study on financing structure notes that real estate financing and financing structure stability can influence credit risk exposure, although the significant effects disappear when controlling for other factors [N5-R3]. This implies that product mix and maturity-related factors matter, but the relationship is not straightforward. The evidence does not provide a direct Malaysian-only breakdown by size or maturity, so those differences remain partially inferred rather than directly established [N2-F2][N5-R3].

Comparisons across Islamic versus conventional banks are mixed but generally consistent with Islamic banks having lower credit risk. The comparative credit-risk study says Islamic banks have significantly lower credit risk than conventional banks [N4-R1], and another comparative study says Islamic banks are less exposed to credit risk compared to conventional banks [N4-R3]. The Indonesian capital buffer study also notes that Islamic banks are distinct because of the core role of PLS financing and higher financing risk [N2-F2]. These findings imply that the relationship between capital buffers and credit risk may differ across bank types: Islamic banks may exhibit lower credit risk for the same capital buffer, or may need higher capital buffers to achieve the same risk reduction [N2-F2][N4-R1][N4-R3].

## 3. How capital ratio affects credit risk

The evidence suggests that higher capital ratios are associated with lower credit risk, but the relationship is often nonlinear and context-dependent [N2-F2][N3-R1][N4-R1][N4-R3]. The Ghana credit-risk study notes that non-performing loans reflect excessive risk concentration and poor portfolio quality, which undermine risk-adjusted returns [N3-R1]. It also says that credit risk management is linked to NPLs, provisioning, and operating costs [N3-F3]. The Indonesian capital buffer study explicitly states that CAR and FDR have a significant positive effect on ROA, indicating that strong capital adequacy and efficient liquidity management improve performance [N2-F2]. While that is performance evidence, it is consistent with the broader logic that higher capital ratios reduce vulnerability to credit losses.

The evidence does not show a clean linear relationship, but it does suggest nonlinear or threshold effects. The Indonesian capital buffer study emphasizes that low competition discourages banks from having a high capital buffer, while stability, bank size, and high financing default encourage higher capital buffers [N2-F2]. It also notes that PLS financing, total financing, and operating inefficiency lower capital buffers [N2-F2]. This implies that the effect of capital ratio on credit risk is not constant across all banks; it depends on bank-specific factors and financing structure. The study further says that Islamic banks are grouped into PLS and non-PLS financing, and that PLS financing is associated with higher financing risk [N2-F2]. Together, these findings suggest a nonlinear relationship: capital ratios matter, but their impact is modified by the bank’s product mix and operational efficiency [N2-F2][N3-F3].

The evidence also indicates that capital ratio interacts with credit growth and asset quality. The Indonesian capital buffer study notes that capital buffers are important for banking soundness and stability, and that Basel III introduced countercyclical and capital conservation buffers to support a strong and resilient banking system [N2-F2]. It also says that capital buffers are used to anticipate losses due to excessive credit growth or financing [N2-F2]. The Ghana study similarly links credit risk to NPLs, provisioning, and operating costs, suggesting that capital adequacy affects the ability to absorb losses and maintain asset quality [N3-F3]. Taken together, these sources support the idea that a higher capital ratio can moderate credit growth and improve asset quality by reducing the need for excessive provisioning and by providing a buffer against losses [N2-F2][N3-F3].

Comparisons across Islamic versus conventional banks show that Islamic banks may have different capital ratio relationships with credit risk. The comparative credit-risk study says Islamic banks have significantly lower credit risk than conventional banks as based on DD [N4-R1], and another comparative study says Islamic banks are less exposed to credit risk compared to conventional banks [N4-R3]. The Indonesian capital buffer study also states that Islamic banks differ because of the core role of PLS financing and higher financing risk [N2-F2]. These findings imply that the capital ratio relationship with credit risk may vary across bank types: Islamic banks may exhibit lower credit risk for the same capital ratio, or may need higher capital ratios to achieve the same risk reduction [N2-F2][N4-R1][N4-R3].

## 4. Malaysian context and limitations

Malaysian Islamic banks operate in a dual-banking environment, where they are subject to both general banking regulation and Shariah-specific requirements [N4-R2][N7-R2]. This structural context matters because it means Malaysian Islamic banks are not treated as a monolithic category, but must be understood alongside conventional banks and the broader regulatory architecture [N4-R2][N7-R2]. Structural and macroeconomic factors that matter alongside capital include financing concentration, sectoral exposure, and macroeconomic conditions. The Malaysian Islamic bank evidence highlights that sectoral financing concentration by Islamic banks in Malaysia has become a recurring issue [N7-R3]. It also notes that credit risk is influenced by bank-specific variables and that empirical results show some bank-specific variables significantly influence credit risk of Malaysia Islamic banks [N7-R1]. The broader macroeconomic evidence indicates that macroeconomic factors can affect credit risk, with one Malaysian study finding that Islamic Financing rate (IFR) stands out as the only factor that had a significant impact on credit risk exposure and non-performing loans [N5-R1][N5-R4]. Taken together, these findings suggest that capital is only one driver of credit risk; financing concentration, sectoral exposure, and macroeconomic conditions also play important roles [N7-R3][N7-R1][N5-R1][N5-R4].

Islamic banking products and risk characteristics differ from conventional banks in several ways. The evidence notes that Islamic banks are shaped by Shariah rules that prohibit riba, require ethical conduct, and link risk sharing to financing instruments [N4-R5]. It also says Islamic banks have Shariah-compliant credit risk-mitigating techniques appropriate for each Islamic financing instrument [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The Indonesian capital buffer study further states that Islamic banks differ because of the core role of PLS financing and the associated financing risk [N2-F2]. In Malaysia, this distinction is reinforced by the comparative analysis of Islamic and conventional banks, which explicitly compares the two systems [N4-R1][N7-R2]. The implication is that Malaysian Islamic banks are not merely conventional banks with Islamic branding; their products, governance, and risk structure are distinct, which affects how credit risk is measured and interpreted [N4-R5][N6-R2][N6-R3][N2-F2].

Study limitations are important for confidence in Malaysian Islamic bank evidence. The upstream risk-indicators report shows that measurement choices can affect conclusions about risk, because Islamic banks use NPLs, provisioning, coverage ratios, and cost of risk, but those indicators are adapted through Shariah-compliant frameworks [N3-R1][N3-R4][N3-R5][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. The Malaysian evidence also suggests that the relationship between capital buffers and credit risk is influenced by bank-specific factors and financing structure, but the evidence is more suggestive than definitive [N2-F2][N5-R3]. The Malaysian empirical study on credit risk says only a few bank-specific variables significantly influence credit risk, which implies that the evidence base may be limited and that not all factors are clearly identified [N7-R1]. Additionally, the evidence does not provide a detailed Malaysian-only estimate of how capital buffers or ratios affect credit risk, so conclusions are partially inferred from broader Islamic banking and comparative studies [N7-R1][N7-R2].

How Malaysian evidence compares with broader Islamic bank studies is mixed. The upstream risk-indicators report shows that Islamic banks are often compared with conventional banks using NPLs as proxies for credit risk, while the literature acknowledges novel approaches [N3-R3][N6-R4]. The comparative credit-risk evidence also indicates that Islamic banks tend to have lower credit risk than conventional banks [N4-R1][N4-R3]. However, the Malaysian evidence is more country-specific than the broader Islamic bank literature. The Malaysian studies on credit risk and financing concentration suggest that Malaysia’s dual-banking context and structural issues such as sectoral financing concentration are important [N7-R3][N7-R2]. At the same time, the broader Islamic banking literature indicates that Islamic banks may differ in product mix, financing risk, and Shariah compliance, which can affect the interpretation of capital and credit-risk relationships [N2-F2][N4-R5]. Overall, the Malaysian evidence is useful but should be read alongside broader Islamic banking studies, with caution about generalizing findings beyond Malaysia’s structural and macroeconomic setting [N5-R1][N5-R4][N7-R1][N7-R2].

## 5. Bottom line

In Malaysian Islamic banks, **capital buffer** and **capital ratio** both matter to credit risk, but in different ways:

- **Capital buffer** acts as a cushion during stress and downturns, and higher buffers are associated with lower credit risk, though the relationship depends on bank-specific factors and financing structure [N2-F2][N3-R1][N4-R1][N4-R3].
- **Capital ratio** reflects adequacy relative to risk-weighted assets, and higher ratios are generally associated with lower credit risk, but the relationship is often nonlinear and can be modified by credit growth, asset quality, and operational efficiency [N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-R1][N4-R3].

Overall, the evidence suggests that both measures help reduce credit risk, but they are not automatic safeguards. Their effects depend on the bank’s product mix, Shariah-compliant governance, and broader structural and macroeconomic conditions in Malaysia [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-F2][N4-R5][N7-R3][N5-R1][N5-R4].

Islamic banking-specific risk indicators and measurement challenges

Islamic banks use credit risk metrics that are broadly similar to conventional banks, but the interpretation and adaptation differ because of Shariah rules and product structure. The most common indicators are non-performing loans (NPLs), provisioning, and related coverage ratios, which are standard across banking systems [N3-R1][N3-R4][N3-R5]. In the evidence provided, NPLs are described as reflecting excessive risk concentration and poor portfolio quality, undermining risk-adjusted returns [N3-R1]. The BBVA source notes that the NPL ratio, coverage ratio, and cost of risk are the three most widely used metrics for measuring credit quality [N3-R4]. The Ghana study also emphasizes that credit risk management is linked to NPLs and other bank-specific factors, including provisioning and operating costs [N3-F3]. Together, these sources show that the core measurement framework is familiar, but its application is context-sensitive.

A key adaptation in Islamic banking is that risk indicators must be interpreted through Shariah-compliant lenses. The evidence on Islamic banks explicitly states that they should have Shariah-compliant credit risk-mitigating techniques appropriate for each Islamic financing instrument [N6-R2][N6-R3]. It also notes that Islamic banks must be aware of Shariah-compliant requirements and that risk management principles include credit, liquidity, and Shariah compliance [N6-R5]. This implies that the same NPL or provisioning figures may not be directly comparable across Islamic and conventional banks if Islamic banks’ products inherently reduce exposure to certain conventional risks. The comparative study of Islamic and conventional banks in Malaysia and other markets says Islamic banks are often compared with conventional banks using NPLs as proxies for credit risk, while the literature also acknowledges novel approaches [N3-R3][N6-R4]. That distinction matters because NPLs alone may not capture the full risk picture when Islamic banks use profit-loss sharing (PLS) and other Shariah-based instruments.

The evidence also shows that Islamic banking products differ from conventional banks in ways that affect measurement. The Malaysian Islamic bank study on financing structure notes that real estate financing and financing specialization can influence credit risk exposure [N5-R3]. The Indonesian capital buffer study explicitly states that Islamic banks differ from conventional banks because of the core role of PLS financing, which is associated with higher financing risk due to moral hazard and asymmetric information [N2-F2]. In contrast, conventional banking is described as interest-based lending, while Islamic banking is shaped by Shariah rules that prohibit riba and require ethical conduct [N4-R5]. These differences mean that a bank’s credit risk cannot be measured in isolation from its product mix: Islamic banks may have lower exposure to interest rate risk, but higher exposure to financing risk or asymmetric information risk.

Measurement choices matter for conclusions about risk. The Ghana study notes that credit risk indicators are often combined with bank-specific characteristics and that the risk-performance nexus is context-dependent [N3-F3]. Overall, the evidence indicates that Islamic banks use similar credit risk indicators as conventional banks, but their interpretation is modified by Shariah rules and product structure. Capital buffer and capital ratio are related but distinct concepts. A capital ratio, such as the capital adequacy ratio (CAR), measures how much capital a bank holds relative to its risk-weighted assets [N1-R1][N1-R3]. The Malaysian capital adequacy framework states that regulatory capital requirements seek to ensure risk exposures are backed by an adequate amount of capital [N1-R1]. In contrast, a capital buffer is capital that exceeds the minimum requirement and is intended to absorb losses during stress or downturns [N2-F2]. The Indonesian capital buffer study explicitly defines capital buffer as capital exceeding the minimum requirement and notes that Basel III introduced countercyclical and capital conservation buffers [N2-F2]. This distinction is important: the ratio measures adequacy, while the buffer measures resilience beyond adequacy.

For Islamic banks, Bank Negara Malaysia’s framework is central. The evidence provided shows that the Malaysian capital adequacy framework is part of the regulatory environment, and Bank Negara Malaysia regulates Islamic banks through capital adequacy requirements [N1-R1][N1-R4]. The Indonesian capital buffer study also notes that the Indonesian Financial Services Authority set a minimum capital adequacy ratio of 8% [N2-F2]. While the evidence does not directly quote Bank Negara Malaysia’s exact minimum for Islamic banks, it does establish that Malaysian Islamic banks operate under capital adequacy rules tied to risk-weighted assets, and that the framework is provided by Bank Negara Malaysia [N1-R1][N1-R4]. The more specific threshold for Islamic banks is therefore indirectly anchored in the same regulatory logic that applies to all Malaysian banks.

The requirements are applied specifically to Islamic banks through Shariah-compliant credit risk-mitigating techniques and product-specific rules. The evidence on Islamic banks says they must have Shariah-compliant credit risk-mitigating techniques appropriate for each Islamic financing instrument [N6-R2][N6-R3]. It also says that Islamic banks must be aware of Shariah-compliant requirements and that risk management includes credit, liquidity, and Shariah compliance [N6-R5]. This means that Islamic banks are not treated as conventional banks in a blanket sense; their capital requirements are implemented within a framework that recognizes their product structure and Shariah constraints. The Indonesian capital buffer study further notes that Islamic banks differ because of the core role of PLS financing and the associated financing risk [N2-F2]. That implies that capital requirements for Islamic banks are not simply a numerical floor, but are adapted to the types of financing and the risk profile they create.

Islamic banking rules do modify the calculation or interpretation, though the evidence is indirect. The framework material emphasizes that Islamic banks are subject to the same capital adequacy rules as other banks, but the comparative credit-risk study notes that Islamic banks are less exposed to credit risk because of stricter ethical and Shariah constraints [N4-R1][N4-R3]. The Indonesian capital buffer study also states that Islamic banks are grouped into PLS financing and non-PLS financing, and that PLS financing is associated with higher financing risk [N2-F2]. Taken together, this suggests that the interpretation of capital adequacy and buffer requirements for Islamic banks is shaped by Shariah-compliant product design and the associated risk characteristics. The evidence does not provide a formal formula for Islamic bank-specific capital buffer or ratio thresholds, but it clearly supports the view that the same regulatory principles are applied with attention to Islamic banking’s distinct structure [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R4][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5].

In practice, then, capital buffer and capital ratio for Islamic banks mean: a capital ratio measures adequacy relative to risk-weighted assets, while a capital buffer measures additional capital beyond the minimum needed to withstand stress [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-F2]. Bank Negara Malaysia imposes these requirements through capital adequacy rules, and Islamic banks are subject to them within a Shariah-compliant framework that adapts the implementation to their product mix and risk profile [N1-R1][N1-R4][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5].

The evidence also indicates that capital buffers moderate credit risk during stress or downturns. The Indonesian capital buffer study explains that the countercyclical buffer is designed to ensure capital buffer movements occur well throughout the business cycle, and the capital conservation buffer is formed outside periods of financial crisis [N2-F2]. This is consistent with the broader idea that capital buffers act as cushions during stress. The Ghana study similarly emphasizes that risk management is essential to stabilizing the sector and preventing crises, especially in fragile economic environments [N3-F3]. Together, these sources suggest that capital buffers help absorb shocks and reduce the likelihood of credit losses when economic conditions worsen.

There are also differences by bank size, maturity, and product mix, but the evidence is more suggestive than definitive. Comparisons across Islamic versus conventional banks are mixed but generally consistent with Islamic banks having lower credit risk. The regulatory thresholds and minimum requirements are indirectly anchored in Bank Negara Malaysia’s capital adequacy framework, which seeks to ensure that risk exposures are backed by an adequate amount of capital [N1-R1][N1-R4]. The evidence does not directly quote Bank Negara Malaysia’s exact minimum for Islamic banks, but it clearly supports the view that the same regulatory principles apply with attention to Islamic banking’s distinct structure [N1-R1][N1-R4]. ## 2. How capital buffer affects credit risk

The evidence suggests that higher capital buffers are associated with lower credit risk, but the relationship is not uniform and depends on how the buffer is defined, the bank’s environment, and whether Islamic banking rules change the interpretation [N2-F2][N3-R1][N4-R1][N4-R3]. The Indonesian capital buffer study explicitly states that low competition discourages banks from having a high capital buffer, while stability, bank size, and high financing default encourage higher capital buffers [N2-F2]. It also says that PLS financing, total financing, and operating inefficiency lower capital buffers [N2-F2]. This implies that a higher capital buffer is not always a direct substitute for lower credit risk; it is influenced by bank-specific factors and financing structure. Still, the general direction is that stronger capital buffers are linked to greater resilience.

On the credit-risk side, the evidence points to credit risk being reduced when banks hold more capital. The Ghana credit-risk study notes that non-performing loans reflect excessive risk concentration and poor portfolio quality, which undermine risk-adjusted returns [N3-R1]. It also says that credit risk management is linked to NPLs, provisioning, and operating costs [N3-F3]. The comparative credit-risk study on Islamic and conventional banks concludes that Islamic banks have significantly lower credit risk than conventional banks as based on DD [N4-R1], and another comparative study says Islamic banks are less exposed to credit risk compared to conventional banks [N4-R3]. The evidence also indicates that capital buffers moderate credit risk during stress or downturns. The Indonesian capital buffer study explains that the countercyclical buffer is designed to ensure capital buffer movements occur well throughout the business cycle, and the capital conservation buffer is formed outside periods of financial crisis [N2-F2]. This is consistent with the broader idea that capital buffers act as cushions during stress. The Ghana study similarly emphasizes that risk management is essential to stabilizing the sector and preventing crises, especially in fragile economic environments [N3-F3]. Together, these sources suggest that capital buffers help absorb shocks and reduce the likelihood of credit losses when economic conditions worsen [N2-F2][N3-F3].

The Malaysian Islamic bank study on financing structure notes that real estate financing and financing structure stability can influence credit risk exposure, although the significant effects disappear when controlling for other factors [N5-R3]. This implies that product mix and maturity-related factors matter, but the relationship is not straightforward. The evidence does not provide a direct Malaysian-only breakdown by size or maturity, so those differences remain partially inferred rather than directly established [N2-F2][N5-R3].

Comparisons across Islamic versus conventional banks are mixed but generally consistent with Islamic banks having lower credit risk. The comparative credit-risk study says Islamic banks have significantly lower credit risk than conventional banks [N4-R1], and another comparative study says Islamic banks are less exposed to credit risk compared to conventional banks [N4-R3]. Together, these findings suggest a nonlinear relationship: capital ratios matter, but their impact is modified by the bank’s product mix and operational efficiency [N2-F2][N3-F3].

The Indonesian capital buffer study notes that capital buffers are important for banking soundness and stability, and that Basel III introduced countercyclical and capital conservation buffers to support a strong and resilient banking system [N2-F2]. Malaysian Islamic banks operate in a dual-banking environment, where they are subject to both general banking regulation and Shariah-specific requirements [N4-R2][N7-R2]. Islamic banking-specific risk indicators and measurement challenges

Islamic banks use credit risk metrics that are broadly similar to conventional banks, but the interpretation and adaptation differ because of Shariah rules and product structure. The most common indicators are non-performing loans (NPLs), provisioning, and related coverage ratios, which are standard across banking systems [N3-R1][N3-R4][N3-R5]. In the evidence provided, NPLs are described as reflecting excessive risk concentration and poor portfolio quality, undermining risk-adjusted returns [N3-R1]. The BBVA source notes that the NPL ratio, coverage ratio, and cost of risk are the three most widely used metrics for measuring credit quality [N3-R4]. The Ghana study also emphasizes that credit risk management is linked to NPLs and other bank-specific factors, including provisioning and operating costs [N3-F3]. Together, these sources show that the core measurement framework is familiar, but its application is context-sensitive.

A key adaptation in Islamic banking is that risk indicators must be interpreted through Shariah-compliant lenses. The evidence on Islamic banks explicitly states that they should have Shariah-compliant credit risk-mitigating techniques appropriate for each Islamic financing instrument [N6-R2][N6-R3]. It also notes that Islamic banks must be aware of Shariah-compliant requirements and that risk management principles include credit, liquidity, and Shariah compliance [N6-R5]. This implies that the same NPL or provisioning figures may not be directly comparable across Islamic and conventional banks if Islamic banks’ products inherently reduce exposure to certain conventional risks. The comparative study of Islamic and conventional banks in Malaysia and other markets says Islamic banks are often compared with conventional banks using NPLs as proxies for credit risk, while the literature also acknowledges novel approaches [N3-R3][N6-R4]. That distinction matters because NPLs alone may not capture the full risk picture when Islamic banks use profit-loss sharing (PLS) and other Shariah-based instruments.

The evidence also shows that Islamic banking products differ from conventional banks in ways that affect measurement. The Malaysian Islamic bank study on financing structure notes that real estate financing and financing specialization can influence credit risk exposure [N5-R3]. The Indonesian capital buffer study explicitly states that Islamic banks differ from conventional banks because of the core role of PLS financing, which is associated with higher financing risk due to moral hazard and asymmetric information [N2-F2]. In contrast, conventional banking is described as interest-based lending, while Islamic banking is shaped by Shariah rules that prohibit riba and require ethical conduct [N4-R5]. These differences mean that a bank’s credit risk cannot be measured in isolation from its product mix: Islamic banks may have lower exposure to interest rate risk, but higher exposure to financing risk or asymmetric information risk.

Measurement choices matter for conclusions about risk. The Ghana study notes that credit risk indicators are often combined with bank-specific characteristics and that the risk-performance nexus is context-dependent [N3-F3]. The same applies to Islamic banks: if NPLs, provisioning, or coverage ratios are used without accounting for product structure, Shariah compliance, or financing specialization, the conclusions may be misleading. The comparative credit-risk study in the evidence says Islamic banks have significantly lower credit risk than conventional banks as based on DD [N4-R1], but it also notes that Islamic banks are less exposed to credit risk partly because of stricter ethical and Shariah constraints [N4-R3]. This suggests that measurement choices—such as which risk proxy is used and whether Shariah-specific factors are controlled for—can shape whether a bank appears riskier or safer. The evidence also shows that credit risk is not only about loan defaults but also about how banks manage provisioning, operating costs, and regulatory capital [N3-R1][N3-R5][N3-F3].

Overall, the evidence indicates that Islamic banks use similar credit risk indicators as conventional banks, but their interpretation is modified by Shariah rules and product structure. NPLs, provisioning, coverage ratios, and cost of risk remain central, but Islamic banks must apply them in ways that recognize PLS financing, financing specialization, and Shariah compliance [N3-R1][N3-R4][N3-R5][N5-R3][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. The risk measurement picture is therefore not simply a matter of numbers; it depends on how the bank’s products and governance are structured [N2-F2][N4-R5].

A capital ratio, such as the capital adequacy ratio (CAR), measures how much capital a bank holds relative to its risk-weighted assets [N1-R1][N1-R3]. In contrast, a capital buffer is capital that exceeds the minimum requirement and is intended to absorb losses during stress or downturns [N2-F2]. The Indonesian capital buffer study explicitly defines capital buffer as capital exceeding the minimum requirement and notes that Basel III introduced countercyclical and capital conservation buffers [N2-F2]. This distinction is important: the ratio measures adequacy, while the buffer measures resilience beyond adequacy.

For Islamic banks, Bank Negara Malaysia’s framework is central. The evidence provided shows that the Malaysian capital adequacy framework is part of the regulatory environment, and Bank Negara Malaysia regulates Islamic banks through capital adequacy requirements [N1-R1][N1-R4]. The Indonesian capital buffer study also notes that the Indonesian Financial Services Authority set a minimum capital adequacy ratio of 8% [N2-F2]. While the evidence does not directly quote Bank Negara Malaysia’s exact minimum for Islamic banks, it does establish that Malaysian Islamic banks operate under capital adequacy rules tied to risk-weighted assets, and that the framework is provided by Bank Negara Malaysia [N1-R1][N1-R4]. The more specific threshold for Islamic banks is therefore indirectly anchored in the same regulatory logic that applies to all Malaysian banks.

The requirements are applied specifically to Islamic banks through Shariah-compliant credit risk-mitigating techniques and product-specific rules. The evidence on Islamic banks says they must have Shariah-compliant credit risk-mitigating techniques appropriate for each Islamic financing instrument [N6-R2][N6-R3]. It also says that Islamic banks must be aware of Shariah-compliant requirements and that risk management includes credit, liquidity, and Shariah compliance [N6-R5]. This means that Islamic banks are not treated as conventional banks in a blanket sense; their capital requirements are implemented within a framework that recognizes their product structure and Shariah constraints. The Indonesian capital buffer study further notes that Islamic banks differ because of the core role of PLS financing and the associated financing risk [N2-F2]. That implies that capital requirements for Islamic banks are not simply a numerical floor, but are adapted to the types of financing and the risk profile they create.

Islamic banking rules do modify the calculation or interpretation, though the evidence is indirect. The Indonesian capital buffer study also states that Islamic banks are grouped into PLS financing and non-PLS financing, and that PLS financing is associated with higher financing risk [N2-F2]. In practice, then, capital buffer and capital ratio for Islamic banks mean: a capital ratio measures adequacy relative to risk-weighted assets, while a capital buffer measures additional capital beyond the minimum needed to withstand stress [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-F2]. Bank Negara Malaysia imposes these requirements through capital adequacy rules, and Islamic banks are subject to them within a Shariah-compliant framework that adapts the implementation to their product mix and risk profile [N1-R1][N1-R4][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5].
